summary: This RFC defines Virtual Subnet Selection options for DHCPv4 and DHCPv6, plus related sub-options in the DHCPv4 Relay Agent Information option. They let clients, relays and proxies tell a DHCP server which virtual subnet (such as a VPN) an address or prefix should come from. It documents existing usage and updates RFC 3046.

plainLanguage.summary: One address office serves many separate neighborhoods. This option is a label on the request saying which neighborhood the new address must come from.

questions: what is dhcp virtual subnet selection
how does dhcp handle vpn address allocation
what is the vss control sub-option
subtitle: DHCP options that tell a server which VPN or virtual subnet an address should be allocated from.

tldr.problem: A DHCP server serving several VPNs needs to know which VPN a client is on, so it can pick an address from the right address space and the reply can be routed back correctly.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a DHCPv4 VSS option, a DHCPv6 VSS option, and two sub-options in the DHCPv4 Relay Agent Information option (VSS and VSS-Control). Each carries a Type and a VPN identifier that the relay, client or server uses to name the VPN.
tldr.outcome: Servers can allocate addresses from multiple independent address spaces. The RFC documents existing DHCPv4 usage, adds DHCPv6, and updates RFC 3046 about copying sub-options.

today: RFC 6607 is a Proposed Standard from April 2012. Per the unit metadata it has not been obsoleted or updated, and it updates RFC 3046 as described above.

sections.title: Why DHCP Needs VPN Information
sections.content:
Virtual Private Network (VPN) use is growing: travelling users who need to appear on the home corporate network, ISPs providing extranet connectivity for customer companies, and so on. In such cases the DHCP server must know the VPN, which the RFC also calls the Virtual Subnet Selector (VSS), from which to allocate an address and other resources.

This memo defines a DHCPv4 VSS option, a DHCPv6 VSS option and two VSS sub-options carried in the DHCPv4 Relay Agent Information option. They are meant for DHCP clients, relay agents and proxy clients. A server that understands them uses the VSS information together with other data to decide the subnet to pick an address from, and also details such as DNS server and default router.

Through a relay, the Relay Agent Information sub-options (DHCPv4) or the DHCPv6 VSS option in Relay-forward and Relay-reply messages carry the information. When a DHCP proxy asks for an address on behalf of another entity, the proxy itself puts the VSS option in its messages. For DHCPv6, everything said about addresses also applies to prefix delegation.
sections.plainLanguage: When many groups share one address office, each request needs to say which group it is for, or the office will not know where to hand out the address.

sections.title: The Options and Sub-Options
sections.content:
Two options and two sub-options are defined. The payload that carries VSS information is identical in all three that hold it.

  • DHCPv4 VSS option: code 221, a one-octet length (minimum 1), then Type and VSS information.
  • DHCPv4 VSS sub-option of the Relay Agent Information option: code 151, same layout.
  • DHCPv4 VSS-Control sub-option: code 152, length 0. In a request it says a VSS sub-option is also present. In a reply it says the server did not understand the VSS sub-option.
  • DHCPv6 VSS option: OPTION_VSS (68), a two-octet option-len (minimum 1), then Type and VSS information. A client or relay agent may include it.

The Type byte says how to read the rest. Type 0 is an NVT ASCII VPN identifier, which MUST NOT be terminated with a zero byte. Type 1 is an RFC 2685 VPN-ID, which is 7 octets long. Type 255 means the global, default VPN: there MUST NOT be any VSS information after the Type and the length MUST be 1. Types 2 to 254 are unassigned.
sections.plainLanguage: The label has a kind (a name, a number, or 'the normal place') followed by the name or number itself. A tiny extra label is used to check whether the office read the first label.

sections.title: Who Decides the VPN
sections.content:
The VSS information tells the relay agent that packets to and from the client must flow over the right VPN, and tells the server which IP address space to allocate from. A server supporting VSS must be ready to configure a separate address space for each VPN. These spaces are typically independent, so the same address bytes could go to one client in the global VPN and to a different client in another VPN without conflict, because the address is qualified by the VPN.

A client, a relay agent or a server could each insert VSS information, but the RFC describes two known paradigms.

Relay assigns the VPN is the typical case. The client knows nothing about the VPN. The relay agent knows the client's VPN and inserts the VSS sub-option and the VSS-Control sub-option (DHCPv4), or a DHCPv6 VSS option in the Relay-forward message. The server uses it to choose the address space.

Server assigns the VPN is the second case. The server is configured to know the client's VPN and sends the VSS sub-option or option back to the relay, which uses it to place the client on the right VPN and then includes VSS information in later requests.

Relay agents and servers MUST support the first approach and SHOULD support the second. They SHOULD NOT be configured to operate both at the same time. Each entity should know through external policy or configuration whether it specifies VSS information, responds to it, or ignores it. Misconfiguration SHOULD result in the client being unable to get an address.
sections.plainLanguage: Usually the doorman (relay) knows which neighborhood a visitor is from and tells the address office. Sometimes the office knows and tells the doorman instead. Everyone must know their own job.

sections.title: Relay Agent and Client Behavior
sections.content:
A relay agent that receives a request from a client on a VPN SHOULD include VSS information before forwarding it, unless configuration or policy says otherwise. A DHCPv4 relay MUST add a VSS sub-option, and a DHCPv6 relay MUST add a VSS option in the Relay-forward message. A DHCPv4 relay MUST also add the zero-length VSS-Control sub-option whenever it adds the VSS sub-option.

The reason is that RFC 3046 says a server should copy all sub-options from a request into the reply. A server that does not understand VSS would just copy the VSS sub-option back, and the relay could not tell whether it was used. If both sub-options come back, the relay MUST assume the server did not act on the VSS information. If only the VSS sub-option comes back, it SHOULD assume the server succeeded. In DHCPv6, the option's appearance in the Relay-reply means the server understood and acted on it.

If a server sends VSS information that the relay cannot honor, for example no matching VPN is configured, the relay MUST drop the packet instead of sending it to the client. A relay may always add a Type 255 option to forestall VSS information from relays or clients closer to the client.

Ordinary clients have no interaction with VSS. An entity talking directly to a server, such as a DHCP proxy or a relay sending a Leasequery, uses the VSS option and MUST include it in every message about an address on a VPN other than the global one. A DHCPv6 client SHOULD place a single VSS option at the same level as the Client Identifier option, and MUST NOT include different VSS options in one message. If a client sends a VSS option and gets none back, or a different value, it SHOULD drop the packet because the address is not in the requested VPN.
sections.plainLanguage: The doorman adds a 'which neighborhood' label plus a tiny test label. If both labels come back, the office did not read them. If only the first comes back, all is well.

sections.title: Server Behavior
sections.content:
A server receiving a VSS option or sub-option SHOULD allocate an address (or access an existing one) from the VPN named. No allocation policy is prescribed. A server may refuse to allocate if it cannot use the VSS information, or fall back to the global VPN, which is also what a server without VSS support appears to do, so clients and relays SHOULD be ready for either.

For the DHCPv4 or DHCPv6 option, a server MUST return the option if it used it to allocate an address, and MUST NOT include it if it cannot or is not configured to support VSS or the requested VPN. It SHOULD return an exact copy unless it wants to change the VPN, in which case it SHOULD use the same Type if possible. Appearance of the code in the Parameter Request List or OPTION_ORO does not change this.

For the DHCPv4 sub-option, a server that supports it MUST copy the VSS sub-option into the outgoing Relay Agent Information option and MUST NOT copy the VSS-Control sub-option. If it used different VSS information, it MUST return that instead. If it supports the sub-option but does not honor it, it MUST NOT echo either sub-option. A server that gets a VSS sub-option without VSS-Control MUST process it the same way.

If conflicting VSS information arrives, the information from the relay agent closest to the server SHOULD win. In DHCPv4 the sub-option takes precedence over the option, and in DHCPv6 the outermost Relay-forward message's option does. The reasoning is that the nearer relay is almost certainly more trusted than the client or more distant relays. The server MUST replicate all VSS options in the response, containing only the VSS information it actually used.
sections.plainLanguage: The office gives out an address from the neighborhood on the label and writes the same label on the reply. If it used a different neighborhood, it writes that one instead, and it believes the doorman closest to it most.

sections.title: The Update to RFC 3046
sections.content:
This document updates Section 2.2 of RFC 3046. The old sentence said that DHCP servers claiming to support the Relay Agent Information option SHALL echo the entire contents of the option in all replies. The new sentence adds an exception: "except if otherwise specified in the definition of specific Relay Agent Information sub-options."

That exception is what lets a VSS-aware server leave the VSS-Control sub-option out of its reply, which is how the relay learns the server understood the VSS sub-option.
sections.plainLanguage: The old rule said 'copy everything back'. The new rule says 'copy everything back, unless a sub-option's own rules say otherwise'.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC points to existing protections: DHCPv4 authentication (RFC 3118) for intradomain use, relay agent authentication (RFC 4030), and the general DHCPv6 threats and authentication described in RFC 3315.

A specific risk is that a client could use the VSS option to obtain an address from any VPN. That allows a more complete address-pool exhaustion attack, since the client is no longer limited to the pools on its local subnet. Servers should use whatever techniques they can to prevent this, for example the giaddr in DHCPv4 or the link address in the DHCPv6 Relay-forward message. One defense is for the relay agent to insert its own VSS option or sub-option to override the client's.

Servers that implement VSS MUST by default disable the feature, so it must be turned on by configuration. A server SHOULD be able to enable it selectively, for example only for explicitly configured client-ids, only for clients on a particular subnet, or restricted to certain VSSs.
sections.plainLanguage: A sneaky visitor could ask for an address from someone else's neighborhood until it runs out. So the feature starts switched off, and the doorman can overwrite the visitor's label.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content:
IANA assigned DHCPv4 option number 221 to the VSS option, in accordance with RFC 3942. It assigned relay agent sub-option 151 to the VSS sub-option. That value was already used by existing implementations, and this document is essentially upward-compatible with them. It assigned 152 to the VSS-Control sub-option and 68 to the DHCPv6 VSS option from the DHCP Option Codes registry.

IANA also created a new sub-registry called "VSS Type Options" for the Type byte, shared by all the options. New values may only be defined by IETF Review, meaning by RFCs approved by the IESG.
sections.plainLanguage: The numbers for the labels were written in an official list, and adding new kinds of labels needs a proper review.
